extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/logic (general educated audience interested in epistemology and metaphysics)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of what can be known about bodies, minds, and attributes: defining 'body' and 'mind' as unknown causes/subjects of sensations and classifying attributes (quality, relation, quantity) as grounded in sensations or states of consciousness. Includes distinctions (likeness, succession, identity) and limits of knowledge about noumena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of external objects limited to sensations and their order
rubrics_metrics.description: All we know of objects is the sensations which they give us, and the order of the occurrence of those sensations; the real nature of the thing in itself (the Noumenon) remains inaccessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by references to Kant and Sir William Hamilton: representations (made of our sensations) are all we can know of objects; the thing-in-itself is an impenetrable mystery. This is advanced as a central epistemic principle: inference about an object's inner nature from its effects is unwarranted (a cause does not resemble its effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Body (substratum) as the unknown external cause of sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: A body is conceived as the unknown external cause (substratum) to which we refer the sensations we experience; we know it only through the sensations it excites and the systematic order among them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes metaphysical debates (e.g., Berkeley) and admits that existence of matter cannot be proved by extrinsic evidence; belief in a substratum is characterized as intuitive and practically unavoidable. The passage also examines the anti-substratum argument (if substratum were annihilated and sensations continued, substratum would be undetectable), showing why philosophers consider the substratum notion as a possible mode of conceiving the law of connection among sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Mind as the unknown recipient/subject of feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Mind is the mysterious sentient subject which feels and thinks — known only by the series of its states of consciousness (sensations, thoughts, emotions, volitions); we cannot know its inmost nature apart from those states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to the definition of Body: mind is the unknown percipient of feelings; 'myself' is a conception distinct from the thoughts (the being that has thoughts) but unknowable except through its states. Any new knowledge about the mind would be only the discovery of additional capacities for feeling, thinking, or willing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes classified into Quality, Quantity, and Relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes (what can be predicated of things) are customarily distributed under three heads: Quality, Quantity, and Relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classification structures subsequent analyses: qualities are grounded on sensations; quantity on differences in sensations related to bulk/degree; relations on facts/phenomena involving more than one object (fundamentum relationis). The classification is treated as exhaustive for purposes of logical treatment in the chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities grounded on sensations (quality ≈ sensation/foundation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When we ascribe a quality (e.g., whiteness) to an object we mean that the presence of that object produces in us a particular sensation — the sensation is the 'foundation' of the quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two views are acknowledged: (1) quality is simply the sensation produced; (2) quality is a power inherent in the object causing the sensation. For logical purposes the author adopts language compatible with both, but emphasizes that the sensation (the foundation) is the only part we can ever prove. Anti-pattern: positing an occult 'power' beyond the observed sensation is unnecessary and akin to invoking occult causes (example: Molière's soporific virtue of opium).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not posit occult causes beyond observed sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no need, after assigning the immediate (observable) cause of a sensation, to suppose an additional occult 'power' to explain how the cause produces the effect; invoking such entities merely restates the fact rather than explains it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the physician who says opium has a 'soporific virtue' — this merely reasserts that opium produces sleep. The text recommends sticking to intelligible causes (the assemblage of phenomena) and treating further metaphysical questions as beyond the bounds of the present science of logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations defined by their fundamentum relationis (fact involving both parties)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation between two things is grounded on some fact or phenomenon (the fundamentum relationis) in which both objects enter as parties concerned; the relation names that fact considered with respect to the two terms (e.g., master/servant grounded on services performed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter enumerates many relation-types (likeness, distance, temporal precedence, causal relations, legal relations) and explains that differences in the character of the constituting fact produce different relations. The fundamentum is typically a series of states of consciousness (intentions, acts, sensations) by which the relation makes itself known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resemblance, succession, and simultaneity are sui generis relations grounded in consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Likeness/unlikeness, antecedence/consequence, and simultaneity are peculiar relations: they are either states of consciousness themselves or our knowledge of them is confined to resemblance/succession/simultaneity among sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These cases do not admit the same kind of analysis as other relations because the 'fact' constituting them is not distinct from the related objects (e.g., succession is not a third thing added to two sensations). The text emphasizes that the feeling of resemblance or of succession is presupposed in any analysis and cannot be reduced further within the science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity grounded in differences of sensations (amount as sensory difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: When two objects differ only in quantity (e.g., a gallon vs ten gallons), the distinction is grounded in a difference in the sensations they excite; quantity is the aspect in which the sensations differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: lifting/seeing/drinking ten gallons produces different sensations than one gallon; yard vs foot rule. The author does not attempt to analyze what the sensory difference 'is' but insists that any assertion of quantitative difference is ultimately grounded in perceptible differences in sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feelings taxonomy and related consequences (sensations, thoughts, emotions, volitions; perception as belief; actions as volitions followed by effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feelings are divided into four sorts—sensations, thoughts, emotions, and volitions; perceptions are a particular kind of belief; actions are volitions followed by effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy underpins the treatment of substances and attributes: bodies make themselves known via sensations; minds via their own states and via effects on other minds. It supports later claims that attributes (of both bodies and minds) are grounded in these states of consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes of minds may be ascribed from their own states or from effects on other minds
rubrics_metrics.description: An attribute of a mind may consist in its habitual internal states (e.g., meditative, cheerful) or in the feelings it excites in other minds (terms of approbation/blame); sometimes a predicate implies both senses (e.g., generous = has certain states and excites approbation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'admirable' implies that contemplation excites admiration (an emotion) and that we approve that sentiment. Thus predicates of character can be twofold: describing internal states and describing the effect on observers. Logical practice must recognize both aspects when predicating such attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about linguistic ambiguity between identity and indistinguishable resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: Common language uses 'same' both for strict identity and for very high degree of resemblance (undistinguishableness), especially in talking about feelings; this ambiguity produces confusion and fallacies if not attended to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by saying the sight gives me the 'same' sensation today as yesterday (actually a distinct but identical-like feeling) or that two persons have the 'same' disease/office (meaning equivalent roles rather than literally the same individual). Archbishop Whately singled out this distinction; logicians should be alert to the ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of an attribute reduces to proving the corresponding sensation or state of consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: For logical purposes the only essential part of asserting a quality or attribute is showing that the corresponding sensation or state of consciousness occurs; once that is proved, the quality is proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that whether one speaks of a 'quality' as a power in the object or as the sensation it produces, the demonstrable element in logic is the sensation (the foundation). Thus empirical or demonstrative proof must target the occurrence of the sensation or state rather than hypothesized hidden powers.
